questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a First-Order Linear ODE Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ can be used to transform the equation 

$$
x\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-y
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(-{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & ={z}^{-2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{z}^{-1} \\ -x{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{-2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{z}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}+\frac{1}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-\frac{1}{x}.$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{3}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{y}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{z}^{2/3}}-{x}^{2}{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{x}^{2}z\end{aligned}
$$

Now we write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

Doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x-3{x}^{2}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}z & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=3{x}^{2}.$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ can be used to transform the equation 

$$
-x\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2}-y
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-x(-{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & ={z}^{-2}-{z}^{-1} \\ x{z}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{-2}-{z}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=\frac{1}{x}.$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y\operatorname{ln}⁡y=xy
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{z}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{z}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{z}=x{e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{z}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & =x{e}^{z} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=1.$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-3}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1/3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{y}^{-4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{3{z}^{4/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3{z}^{4/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{4/3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\frac{1}{{z}^{1/3}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3z\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3z\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y=\frac{4{x}^{2}}{y}\,,\,y>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,⟹\,y={(z+{x}^{2})}^{1/2}\,.
$$

]
Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x).
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x)+(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2} & =\frac{4{x}^{2}}{(z+{x}^{2})^{1/2}} \\ x(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x)+2(z+{x}^{2}) & =8{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2x+\frac{2}{x}(z+{x}^{2}) & =8x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2/x\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot 4x \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & ={x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}} \\ {y}^{2} & =2{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+\frac{C}{{x}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $y>0.$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=8x{y}^{1/2}-\frac{4}{x}y\,,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{1/2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1/2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{1/2}}\frac{dy}{dx}\,⟹\,\frac{dy}{dx}=2z\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2z\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =8xz-\frac{4}{x}{z}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =4x-\frac{2}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z & =4x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=4x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (4x) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =4{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z) & =4{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}z)\,\text{d}x & =\int 4{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{2}z & ={x}^{4}+C \\ z & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{1/2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2} & =\frac{{x}^{4}+C}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\frac{({x}^{4}+C)^{2}}{{x}^{4}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
2(1+{x}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{y}-2xy\,,\,y>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{2}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/2}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2{z}^{1/2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(1+{x}^{2})}{{z}^{1/2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{1/2}}-2x{z}^{1/2} \\ (1+{x}^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-2xz\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+{x}^{2})\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-2xz \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}-\frac{2xz}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,z & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2x/(1+{x}^{2})dx} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2})} \\  & =1+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)=1+{x}^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+{x}^{2})\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,z) & =(1+{x}^{2})\cdot (\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}) \\ (1+{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[z(1+{x}^{2})] & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[z(1+{x}^{2})]\,\text{d}x & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ z(1+{x}^{2}) & =x+C \\ z & =\frac{x+C}{1+{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =\frac{x+C}{1+{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\sqrt{\frac{x+C}{1+{x}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

where in the last step we used that $y>0.$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{x}
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{z}^{-1}+2{x}^{2}{z}^{-2}}{x} \\ -\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{xz}+\frac{2x}{{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-2x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-2x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-2{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int 2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x} \\ y & =\frac{3x}{C-2{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation.

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}={y}^{2}-y
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution* $z={y}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}-\frac{1}{z} \\ -\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-1+z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-1,\,Q(x)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{-x}$ yields:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{-x}\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}-z) & ={e}^{-x}\cdot (-1) \\ {e}^{-x}\frac{dz}{dx}-{e}^{-x}z & =-{e}^{-x} \\ \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-x}) & =-{e}^{-x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(z{e}^{-x})\,dx\, & =-\int {e}^{-x}\,dx \\ z{e}^{-x} & ={e}^{-x}+C \\ z & =1+C{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =1+C{e}^{x} \\ y & =\frac{1}{1+C{e}^{x}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}=3{y}^{4}+2xy,\,y(1)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}\,z=-\frac{9}{{x}^{2}}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-3}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-3}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}z=-\frac{9}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{6}{x},\,Q(x)=-\frac{9}{{x}^{2}}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 6/x\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{6\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{6}} \\  & ={x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{6}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{6}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{6}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{6}\cdot (-\frac{9}{{x}^{2}}) \\ {x}^{6}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+6{x}^{5}z & =-9{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{6}z] & =-9{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{6}z]\,\text{d}x & =\int -9{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{6}z & =-\frac{9}{5}{x}^{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-9{x}^{5}}{5{x}^{6}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5{C}_{1}.$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-3}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-3} & =\frac{C-9{x}^{5}}{5{x}^{6}} \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{5{x}^{6}}{C-9{x}^{5}} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{5{x}^{6}}{C-9{x}^{5}}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

From the initial condition  $y(1)=\frac{1}{2}$ we determine $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{5}{C-9}} \\ \frac{1}{8} & =\frac{5}{C-9} \\ C-9 & =40 \\ C & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{5{x}^{6}}{49-9{x}^{5}}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}+x{y}^{2},\,y(1)=2,\,x>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation*

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x
$$

*using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{dz}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-x) \\ x\cdot \frac{dz}{dx}+z & =-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dx}(xz) & =-{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dx}(xz)\,dx & =-\int {x}^{2}dx \\ xz & =-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Now, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x} \\ y & =\frac{3x}{C-{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition $y(1)=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{3}{C-1}\,⟹\,C=\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{3x}{(\frac{5}{2}-{x}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{6x}{5-2{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y(y-1)}{x}=0,\,y(-1)=2,\,x<0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation*

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}-\frac{1}{x}z=-\frac{1}{x}
$$

*using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{dz}{dx}-\frac{z}{x}=-\frac{1}{x}\,.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|x{|}^{-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{|x|} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x<0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=-\frac{1}{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z) & =-\frac{1}{x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{x}) \\ -\frac{1}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}z & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}z) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x}z)\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{x}z & =\frac{1}{x}+C \\ z & =1+Cx.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =1+Cx \\ y & =\frac{1}{1+Cx}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition $y(-1)=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{1}{1-C}\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{(1+\frac{1}{2}x)} \\  & =\frac{2}{2+x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{y(y-1)}{x}=0,\,y(1)=5,\,x>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{x}
$$

using the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={y}^{-1}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{1}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int 1\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =x+C \\ z & =\frac{x+C}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{x+C}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{x+C}\end{aligned}
$$

We now determine $C$ from the initial condition  $y(1)=5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =\frac{1}{1+C}\,⟹\,C=-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{x}{(x-\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =\frac{5x}{(5x-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Solve the initial value problem

$$
x\frac{dy}{dx}+(x+1)y=\frac{3}{xy},\,y(1)=\sqrt{3},\,x>0,\,y>0.
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the fact that the given differential equation can be transformed into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z=6
$$

using the substitution $z={x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
The substitution $z={x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ transforms the given equation into the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z=6.
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=2,\,Q(x)=6\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={e}^{2x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 6 \\ {e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2{e}^{2x}z & =6{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{2x}z) & =6{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{2x}z)\,\text{d}x & =6\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{2x}z & =3{e}^{2x}+C \\ z & =3+C{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{2} & =3+C{e}^{-2x} \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{3+C{e}^{-2x}}{{x}^{2}} \\ y & =\frac{\sqrt{3+C{e}^{-2x}}}{x}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where we used that $x>0$ and $y>0.$

From the initial condition $y(1)=\sqrt{3}$ we determine $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & =\frac{\sqrt{3+C{e}^{-2}}}{1}\,⟹\,C=0\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a First-Order Linear ODE Using a Substitution
canonical_examples.problem:
The substitution $z= y^2$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} = \dfrac{x+2}{2y} + 2x^2y
$$

into an equation of the form $z'(x) + P(x)z(x) = Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2z^{1/2}}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2{z}^{1/2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2}{2{z}^{1/2}}+2{x}^{2}{z}^{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =x+2+4{x}^{2}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-4{x}^{2}z & =x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x) = - 4x^2.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the general solution to the following first-order ODE using the substitution $z=y^3.$

$$
xy^2\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} = x^2+y^3
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's make a substitution

$$
z=y^3\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}=3y^2\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^2\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

 Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{3}\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}\right)=x^2+z
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3}{x}({x}^{2}+z) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3x+\frac{3}{x}z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{x}\,z & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=-\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=3x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (-3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{-3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{x}\,z) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot 3x \\ \frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{3}{{x}^{4}}\,z & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{z}{{x}^{3}}) & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{z}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\ \frac{z}{{x}^{3}} & =-\frac{3}{x}+C \\ z & =-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z=y^3.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =z \\ {y}^{3} & =-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{-3{x}^{2}+C{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the specific solution of the first-order ODE

$$
xe^y\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}+e^y = e^{x} \, ,
$$

given that $y(1)=1$ and $x>0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's make a substitution

$$
z=e^y\,.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ with the chain rule, we get $\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}=e^y\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$ Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of  $z$ as follows:

$$
x\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}+z=e^x\,,
$$

with the initial condition

$$
z(1)=e^{y(1)}=e^1=e\,.
$$

Notice that the left-hand side of the differential equation is now an exact derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & ={e}^{x} \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x}\text{d}x \\ xz & ={e}^{x}+C \\ z & =\frac{{e}^{x}+C}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we determine the value of $C$ that satisfies the initial condition $z(1)=e\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}z(1) & =e \\ \frac{{e}^{1}+C}{1} & =e \\ e+C & =e \\ C & =0\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have 

$$
z  =   \frac{e^x}{x}\,.
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by substituting the solution into $z=e^y.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y} & =z \\ {e}^{y} & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{x} \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{{e}^{x}}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) \\  & =x-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,,\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$ So, the final solution is

$$
y = x - \ln (x), \quad x > 0.
$$
